question.worked_solution:
Notice that the numerator is proportional to the derivative of the denominator, because

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({cos}^{3}⁡x+1)=-3{cos}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

So, let $u={cos}^{3}⁡x+1.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-3{cos}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,⟹\,-\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u={cos}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $0$ | $\pi /3$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $2$ | $9/8$ |

We now substitute and evaluate, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x{cos}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{3}⁡x+1}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\frac{1}{{cos}^{3}⁡x+1}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡x{cos}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{9/8}\frac{1}{u}\cdot (-\frac{1}{3})\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{2}^{9/8}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|{|}_{2}^{9/8} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{9}{8})-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{9}{8})) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{2}{(\frac{9}{8})}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{16}{9})\end{aligned}
$$
